title: Ethiopian Berbere — Home Blend
localName: ቤት ሠራ በርበሬ — Bet Sera Berbere
community: All of Ethiopia — the family berbere recipe
author: Mama Tigist

heritage.origin: All of Ethiopia — every family guards their berbere recipe
heritage.history: Berbere (also written bərbərē) is the spice blend that defines Ethiopian cuisine more than any other single element. While ETH091 gives the standard recipe, the home berbere (bet sera berbere) is the recipe each Ethiopian family passes down through generations — the specific ratios, the choice of chilli varieties, the inclusion or exclusion of certain spices, the roasting technique. Ethiopian grandmothers measure berbere by feel, not by spoon. This version includes the wet-paste form (ye-berbere qimat) used for wats and the dry powder form, both made from scratch with whole dried chillies.

desc: Ethiopian Home Berbere — whole dried chillies toasted and ground with fenugreek, coriander, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, rue, and allspice. The family-recipe berbere — slightly different from the standard blend, with more chilli depth and the option to make it as a wet paste (ye-berbere qimat) for immediate use in wats.
longDesc: Home berbere starts from whole dried chillies rather than chilli powder — the difference is significant. Toasting whole chillies develops complexity that pre-ground powder cannot match. This recipe also includes the wet-paste version (ye-berbere qimat) made by mixing the dry blend with a little water and oil — used directly in wats without pre-blooming.
ingredients: 10 dried guajillo or ancho chillies — mild base
½ tsp dried rue (tena adam) or thyme
// For wet paste: 2 tbsp water + 1 tbsp oil
steps: Remove stems and seeds from dried chillies.
Toast chillies in a dry pan over medium heat, turning, 3—4 minutes until fragrant and slightly darkened. Do not burn.
Toast fenugreek seeds alone: 2 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Toast coriander, cumin, and peppercorns together: 2 minutes.
Grind chillies to a fine powder.
Add all remaining ground spices, herbs, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and salt.
Grind to a uniformly fine powder.
For wet paste: mix 4 tbsp dry berbere with 2 tbsp water and 1 tbsp oil. Add to wats directly.
Store dry blend in an airtight jar away from light.
chefTips: Toast whole chillies from scratch — vastly superior to pre-ground powder.
Fenugreek must be toasted separately: it reaches its optimum at a different time from other seeds.
The wet paste form is what many Ethiopian grandmothers use — it allows direct addition to sauces without a separate blooming step.
Make a large batch — berbere improves over 2—3 weeks as the flavour compounds integrate.
The ratio of mild to hot chillies is adjustable — this is a medium-hot blend.
commonMistakes: Burning the chillies — produces bitter acrid flavour.
Not cooling before grinding — steam in the grinder produces clumps.
Under-toasting fenugreek — raw fenugreek is unpleasantly bitter.
cookingScience: Whole chilli toasting produces Maillard reactions on the chilli flesh — converting the raw green-grassy flavour compounds to hundreds of complex aromatic molecules. This transformation is why home-made berbere from whole chillies is dramatically more complex than commercial powder. The fenugreek's bitter sotolone converts partially to the pleasant caramel-curry character only through sufficient toasting.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian chillies grown domestically — no imports needed for authentic berbere.
servedWith: In every Ethiopian wat and tibs
As the foundation of the entire cuisine
storage: Dry blend: airtight jar, cool dark place — up to 1 year. Wet paste: refrigerate 2 weeks.
healthBenefits: Capsaicin — thermogenic, anti-inflammatory, promotes endorphin release.
Collectively: one of the most antioxidant-dense spice blends in the world.
culturalNote: Every Ethiopian family's berbere is different — the specific ratios, the chilli varieties, the choice to include or exclude certain spices, the roasting depth. This recipe is a starting point, not a prescription. The Ethiopian grandmother who makes the best berbere in her neighbourhood never measures — she has made it hundreds of times. Your berbere will get better with every batch.
